Lissajous/spirograph forms change between frames: a magenta rosette, then a green Möbius-like twist, then a tilted green disc. This shows a choreographed progression, not one repeated layout
Deliberate, unusual palette: monochrome blood-red photography against a black ground with magenta and acid-green line work

Typography with a point of view: an outlined slab-serif title, small caps for roles against large caps for names, and a ragged right-aligned credit stack that sits against the spiral as a counterweight

gaps: This is the benchmark entry, so there is no gap above it

The flat black grounds in the mid-section are austere next to the photographic eye frames, and a little more texture there would connect the two worlds

gaps: No visible typography, and the absence does not serve a concept the way A's integrated credits do. A typographic or graphic system is needed to give the piece a signature

Monochrome red tint on the face, then magenta and acid-green line figures on black. The palette is deliberate, strange and unsettling
Wide slab-serif outline type for the title and the director's name, credits stacked to the right against a figure on the left; scale contrast and placement change from card to card
The film opens and closes on the eye, and the spirals change form and colour from card to card (pink rosette to green twisted ribbon), so the frames show real choreography
This is Saul Bass's title sequence for Vertigo (1958), credited on screen; it is the canonical reference for the form

The black interstitial cards are flat and lack the photographic texture of the eye frames
The spirals are clean mechanical drawings with no material quality, which is by design

gaps: There is no idea: it needs a single concept that links the frames and gives the viewer something to remember (compare A's eye-to-spiral)

defects: Shots are 4.7 s on median and up to 7.5 s long. Most of that is the camera drifting slowly over a formation that is barely changing, so there are long stretches of near-dead air (per-second change drops to 11–16 between about 11 s and 18 s).

Every marcher is the same sprite on a strict grid and they move in lockstep. There is no offset, no per-row delay and no follow-through, so the band looks like a copied array rather than a group of people.
The yellow tuba bells and white instrument rectangles are flat, untextured shapes. Next to the textured grass and soft shadows they look unfinished.
Instruments and shadows jump between frames in the pairs (row 1: white to gold rectangles; row 3: the shadow lattice). That reads as stepped colour or position changes rather than motion with blur.
In the concentric-ring frame, a hard-edged light-green panel intrudes at the right edge. It looks like an unplanned transition or a compositing artifact.

In the 'ANIKIT' end card the letterforms are only implied by marcher dots, with ragged spacing, and 'VIDEO' is a separate serif set flat on top. The two type treatments don't match, and the end card doesn't hold up as a finished lockup.
Middle frames, such as the swirl formation, are crowded and have no single focal point. Separate frames would not work as posters.
gaps: Choreography: top marching-band and crowd-sim pieces move formations with follow-the-leader waves, staggered peels and counter-marches timed to the beat. Here each block translates rigidly and the camera drift does most of the work. The piece needs moves that resolve on hits, followed by real holds.

Pacing and edit: the riser and drop at about 19–23 s is the only real structural event. Shots should be cut to around 2 s and hard-cut on the drum accents, with the formation change between shots acting as the transition, instead of slow dissolves and pans.

Sound: the spectrogram shows a steady, unvaried percussion grid, a single white-noise riser and a thin outro. There is no layered brass, no crowd or field ambience, and no foley for footsteps or instrument hits. Marching-band subject matter is asking for detailed, foley-led sound design.
